1.pericope_label: Behold what manner of love the Father hath bestowed

schools.summary: Calvin makes the adoption gratuitous and argues the point closely: the word for bestowed means it comes from mere bounty and benevolence, so the love is declared to be free, and against the sophists who say God foresees those worthy to be adopted he answers that in that case the gift would not be gratuitous — for why are we sons, except that God began to love us freely when we deserved hatred? He prefers children to sons as the rendering, notes that being called sons is no idle expression since God with his own mouth declares us such, and gives the history behind the address, that the ten tribes were placed by the Assyrian king in various parts and afterwards moved as kingdoms revolved. He also treats the world's ignorance of believers as a trial to faith, since it can hardly be inferred from our present state that God is a Father to us, and gives Isaac and Jacob as the example, both chosen by God yet persecuted by Ishmael and Esau.

Henry finds it strange that the holy God is not ashamed to be called our Father — we who by nature are heirs of sin and by practice children of disobedience and ingratitude — and that the Father adopts all the children of the Son. On the world's ignorance he draws out what it misses: little does it think that these poor, humble, contemned ones are the favourites of heaven, and the disciples may bear it the better since their Lord was here unknown as well as they.

Clarke thinks whole volumes might be written on this verse and the two following without exhausting the subject, and observes that the apostle does not attempt to describe it but calls on the world and the church to behold it; the interrogative adjective asks what great love, both as to quantity and quality. He insists that the verb in the last clause means to acknowledge or approve rather than merely to know of, since the world knew well enough that such persons existed but did not approve of them, a use common in both Testaments; and he notes the parenthesis in the older manuscripts, and we are, which he finds in a long list of versions. Wesley puts the world's failure in two strokes: they know not what to make of us, we are a mystery to them.

Robertson supplies the grammar, noting that the word is a qualitative interrogative found only here in this writer and originally asking of what country or race a thing is, and that the perfect tense marks a completed endowment of the receiver; he quotes Brooke's judgment that the appeal is an effort to restore the waning enthusiasm of the readers, and calls the parenthetical and we are a reflection characteristic of this writer, omitted by the received text. Barnes divides the love in kind and in degree — in kind the most tender and ennobling, in degree the most exalted — and compares a prince who should adopt a wandering, ragged orphan found in the streets, though even that would be a trifle beside what is meant here.

debates.question: Does the world's failure to know believers mean ignorance or disapproval?

positions.position: disapproval — the world knew well enough that such persons existed but did not acknowledge or approve them
a trial to faith rather than a fact about the world: our present state gives the devil his opportunity to obscure the benefit, as with Isaac and Jacob

outliers.note: uses the verse against the doctrine of foreseen worthiness, holding that if God adopted those he foresaw to be worthy the gift would not be gratuitous at all

themes: why the world does not know believers

2.pericope_label: Now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the stages of the adoption: it is secret in God's predestination and in the covenant of grace, open in regeneration, through faith in Christ and by the testimony of the Spirit. Calvin's point is that we act foolishly when we estimate what God has given us by the present state of things, since as to the body we are dust and a shadow with death always before our eyes; he reads the conditional particle as an adverb of time and takes the verb of Christ rather than of our estate, comparing Paul's word that our life is hid with Christ in God. On the promise of seeing him he raises the objection that the wicked shall also see his glory, and answers that the promise is of seeing him as a friend, which will not be their case — they will be filled with terror, as Adam dreaded God's presence and as God told Moses that no man shall see him and live; so far as the image of God is renewed in us we have eyes prepared to see him. He enters one caution besides: the likeness is not equality, since there must be some difference between head and members.

Clarke reads the clause of the second coming, when Christ shall be manifested in his glorified human nature to judge the world, and remarks that this writer had already seen that glory on the mount, where it must have been partly obscured since the disciples were not then like him and could not have borne the sight; he expects to see him in the splendour of his majesty, in the glory of both natures. Wesley adds that it does not yet appear even to ourselves, and says the sight will be manifest and without a veil, and will transform us into the same likeness, the glory of God penetrating our inmost substance.

Barnes takes the present dignity to be worth dwelling on for its own sake, and offers two conjectures why the rest is withheld — that the coming state may be so unlike the present that no words would convey it, and that under a probation no more light may be furnished, lest we cease to be stimulated toward a world of light; on the seeing he holds that there is an influence in beholding the Saviour which tends to transform us. Robertson makes something of the opening adverb, that dignity and duty are ours now without waiting for the second coming, and notes that the pronoun in the hidden clause is neuter, asking what rather than who — which, as Bengel says, suggests something unspeakable contained in the likeness of God; on the subject of the verb he leaves the choice open between Christ and the manifestation, thinking it the better rendering.

debates.question: Who or what is it that shall appear?

positions.position: Christ, at his second coming, manifested in his glorified human nature
either will do, but the neuter it reads better than he — the reference may be to the manifestation just mentioned

outliers.note: answers the objection that the wicked will also see Christ's glory by distinguishing the sight of a friend from the sight that terrifies, and adds that likeness to Christ is not equality with him

3.pericope_label: Every man that hath this hope purifieth himself

schools.summary: Gill says a true hope of the happiness that lies in likeness to Christ and in the vision of him is founded only on his person, blood, righteousness and sacrifice, and is not a hope every man has, being implanted in regeneration and bestowed as a free grace gift. Calvin draws the inference the verse is making, that the desire for holiness should not grow cold because our happiness has not yet appeared, for the hope is sufficient — and though we have not Christ before our eyes, hoping in him cannot but stimulate us to follow purity, since it leads us straight to a perfect pattern of it.

Henry turns the verse into a test of the hope rather than of the effort, since the sons of God know their Lord is of purer eyes than to allow anything impure to dwell with him: it is the hope of hypocrites that makes allowance for gratifying impure desires.

Clarke denies that the reflexive verb means a man purifies his own heart, which is impossible, and takes it of persevering in the purity into which the Lord has brought him, or of anxiously using all the means that lead to it while imploring God for the sanctifying Spirit. On the measure set by the last clause he argues hotly for entire deliverance from sin in this life: if the blood of Christ cleanses from all sin, and he was manifested to destroy the works of the devil, and sin is the work of the devil, then God means that believers shall be saved from all sin. He asks those who deny it how much sin a man may be saved from, since the soul must have a determinate object in view; charges the Westminster divines with laying every man under a fatal necessity of sinning in thought, word and deed; calls it a miserable salvo to say the regenerate sin less than they used to and only occasionally; and asks whether the grace that saved them partially could not save them perfectly.

Barnes will not let the reflexive verb be read as independence — he does not deny that we depend on divine aid — but says the writer brings the agency of man into view as essentially connected with success. Against the perfectionist reading he argues that the passage cannot teach sinless perfection in this life, because whatever it proves it proves of every one who has the hope, so the doctrine would be not that some Christians may become perfect but that all in fact do, which he presumes nobody will hold; what it establishes is that the tendency of the hope is to make a man pure, that all who cherish it will aim at the Saviour's purity, and that the aim will at some future time be accomplished — the same kind of purity here, the same degree hereafter. Robertson gives the word's history, that it was used of ceremonial purifications before the internal cleansing of heart and soul and self, calls the process the work of both God and man, and notes that the emphatic demonstrative refers to Christ, who can be called pure in virtue of the perfection of his humanity.

debates.question: Does the standard as he is pure mean a purity attainable in this life?

positions.position: yes — the blood of Christ cleanses from all sin, and to deny it is to allow grace less power than a heathen's philosophy
no — whatever the verse proves it proves of every believer alike, so it would make perfection universal, which nobody holds; the aim is present, the attainment future

outliers.note: tests the hope rather than the performance, holding that a hope which makes allowance for impure desires is by that fact the hope of a hypocrite

themes: whether sinless purity is attainable here

4.pericope_label: Sin is the transgression of the law

schools.summary: Gill grants the words are true of any sin great or small taken with what follows, but says what is designed here is a course of sinning, a wilful, obstinate persisting in it. Calvin supplies the excuse he thinks was being made — it is no wonder if we sin, because we are men, and there is a great difference between sin and iniquity — which the definition dissipates, since the word for sin may seem light while transgression of the law cannot appear so easily forgiven. But he is careful what the definition does not do: it does not make all sins equal, and has nothing in common with the delirious paradoxes of the Stoics; nor does it mean offending in some instance, since the faithful, still tempted by the lusts of the flesh, are not free from sin and yet are not guilty of iniquity, because sin does not reign in them. To do or practise sin is in this writer's language what being the servant of sin is in his Gospel, a prevailing and habitual course.

Henry defines sin as a privation of agreement with the divine law — that law which is the transcript of the divine nature, contains God's will for the government of the world, and shows man the way of felicity and peace — so that the commission of sin is the rejection of the law, and thereby of the divine authority, and consequently of God himself. He adds that the design of the argument is to fill the believer's mind with multiplied reasons against sin and against all communion with the unfruitful works of darkness.

Clarke widens the reach of the definition by the law's own summary — the spirit of the law as of the gospel is that we should love God with all our powers and our neighbour as ourselves, and since all disobedience is contrary to love, sin is transgression whether the act refers to God or to our neighbour. Wesley puts the aggravation in a clause, that by sinning a man sets God's authority at nought, which is implied in the very nature of sin.

Robertson notes that the article stands with both subject and predicate, making the terms coextensive and so interchangeable: sin is lawlessness and lawlessness is sin; and the participle is present, meaning the habit of doing sin. Barnes reconstructs the setting that made the point necessary, since the writer seems to be combating an opinion then current that men might sin and yet be true Christians; he lists the possible grounds — that orthodoxy was all religion required, that nobody expected men to become holy in this life, that Christ came to relax the law and the freedom he procured was freedom to indulge, that Christians as heirs of all things had a right to enjoy all things, or that the passions are too strong to restrain — all held under some form of Antinomianism. He adds that the law measures our duty and so the degree of guilt when it is not obeyed, embracing what we omit where a thing is commanded as well as what we do where it is forbidden.

debates.question: Does the definition make all sins equal?

positions.position: no — it teaches that sin arises from contempt of God and violates the law, but the doctrine has nothing in common with the Stoic paradoxes
the question does not arise, since the tense describes a habit and not an act

outliers.note: reads the verse as polemical rather than definitional, reconstructing five distinct Antinomian grounds on which men of the time may have held that a Christian might sin freely

themes: a course of sinning rather than a single act

5.pericope_label: He was manifested to take away our sins, and whosoever abideth in him sinneth not

schools.summary: Gill takes the manifestation to be the incarnation itself, the Word who lay in the Father's bosom from all eternity made manifest in the flesh, assuming our nature into union with his divine person; and he fills out what abiding is, as the branch in the vine, deriving light and life and grace from Christ, rooted and grounded in him. Calvin argues that the taking away meant here is not remission: elsewhere Christ takes away sins because he atoned for them so that they are not imputed, but here he really and actually takes them away, since through him our old man is crucified and his Spirit by repentance mortifies the flesh — and the context requires that sense, since those who cease not to sin render void the benefits of Christ. He adds that the writer speaks not of Christ personally but of his whole body, that the renewal is not instantaneous but continues throughout life, and that faith in Christ is vainly pretended where there is no newness of life, for Christ is never dormant where he reigns and puts sin to flight as the sun drives away darkness.

Clarke sets out three things taken away — the power of sin destroyed, its guilt pardoned, its pollution cleansed — and asks whether Christ can be supposed unable or unwilling to accomplish the object of his own coming. On the denial that follows he takes the tense in the last clause as a Hebrew preterite standing for a present: he who sins against God does not see him, the eye of his faith being darkened so that he no longer knows God as his portion. Wesley wants the whole destroyed, root and branch, and reads the clause about Christ's own sinlessness to mean that he could not suffer on his own account but only to make us as himself.

Robertson confirms that the verb refers to the incarnation and not the second coming, though it is the same form used a few lines earlier, and presses the verb for taking away: Isaiah uses a word for bearing sins, but this one means to lift up and carry off, and the noun is plural rather than collective. On the denial he supplies the grammar the argument needs — both verbs are linear presents, so the sense is does not keep on sinning, and the articular participle describes one who lives a life of sin rather than the occasional acts an aorist would name. Barnes calls the appearing the second argument of the paragraph and perhaps the strongest that can bear on a Christian's mind, since the whole work was designed to deliver us from the dominion of sin and not to furnish means of indulgence; and against the perfectionist reading of the denial he brings three objections — that it would make every Christian perfect, that this is untrue of Abraham or Moses or David or Paul, and that the language is such as any writer would use to say a man is not characteristically a sinner.

debates.question: Is the taking away of sins remission or mortification?

positions.position: mortification: the old man is crucified and the flesh put to death, since the argument is that those who go on sinning void the benefit
the vocabulary itself points to removal — the verb means to lift up and carry off, not to bear
all three at once — power destroyed, guilt pardoned, pollution cleansed

outliers.note: argues from the universality of the statement rather than from grammar, holding that a perfectionist reading would prove all Christians sinless or none

themes: in what sense one who abides does not sin

7.pericope_label: He that committeth sin is of the devil

schools.summary: Gill names the deceit guarded against as the Gnostic one, that knowledge without practice is enough and it is no matter how a man lives provided his notions are right; and he is careful that the next sentence not be read of any single act, since then every man would be of the devil, no man living without sin — what is meant is the man who makes sin his constant business, and who is of the devil not by generation but by imitation, resembling him as children do their parents. Calvin uses the verse to deny any middle condition, since Satan reigns wherever the righteousness of Christ has not the primacy, but refuses the Manichean inference, since the devil is not wicked by nature but became so through defection, is not equal to God, and can do nothing except at the permission of his Creator; the beginning meant is not eternity, as when the Word is said to be from the beginning, but that the devil has been an apostate since the creation. He also makes newness of life the test of profession, since many persuade themselves they have righteousness buried in their hearts while iniquity occupies their feet and hands and tongue and eyes, and answers the perfectionists — Pelagians and Catharians formerly made a wrong use of this passage, and some Anabaptists have renewed the dotage.

Clarke hears two deceits — either that you cannot be saved from sin in this life, or that sin cannot alter your state once you are adopted — and answers that a man is righteous according to his state and nature and the extent of his moral powers, allowing for the disparity between what is bounded and what is without limits. He turns the doctrine of the devil's beginning into a charge, that the devil maintains sin in the world by persuading men they cannot be saved from their sins in this life, so as to secure a residence in their hearts, knowing that if he has a place there through life he will probably have it at death. Wesley states the rule in a line, that none is righteous but he who uniformly practises righteousness.

Robertson reads the imperative as continuous — let no one keep on leading you astray — and tells the readers to break the spell of any Gnostic charmer; on the devil's sinning he finds a linear progressive present, meaning he has been sinning from the beginning of his career, this being his normal life, though the conflict ends in certain victory over him. Barnes takes the maxim about doing righteousness as great and undeniable and presses it against every substitute: no matter how a man claims to be justified by faith, how he conforms to the rites of religion, how zealous he is for orthodoxy, what raptures he has had or how little he fears death, unless he is in fact righteous he cannot be a child of God. He allows the following sentence two senses — all who sin resemble Satan so far as they are imperfect, but the principal idea is that all who habitually sin belong to him — and denies that the devil sinned from the beginning of his existence, since he was made holy like the other angels.

debates.question: Does the devil's sinning from the beginning mean from the beginning of his existence?

positions.position: no — he was made holy like the other angels; the sense is that he introduced sin and has practised it ever since
no — the beginning here is the creation of the world, not eternity as when the Word is said to be from the beginning
the tense settles it: a linear present meaning he has been sinning from the beginning of his career as the devil

outliers.note: makes the doctrine of inevitable sinning itself a stratagem of the devil, by which he secures a lodging in the heart for life and so, he hopes, at death

themes: when the devil began to sin

9.pericope_label: Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin, for his seed remaineth in him

schools.summary: Augustine states the difficulty as a pastoral emergency before anyone tries to solve it. A man is pressed by two sayings out of the same letter: if he confesses himself a sinner he fears to hear that he is therefore not born of God; but if he says he has no sin he takes a blow from the other side, that we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. Placed in the midst, he cannot find what to say or confess. Augustine's first move is to close off one exit — to profess oneself without sin is not only full of peril but full of error, and would that a man had none and could say so truly.

Gill describes the birth rather than the difficulty, a being quickened and made partaker of the divine nature, owing not to the will of men but to grace, ascribed sometimes to the Father, sometimes to Christ who quickens whom he will, and chiefly to the Spirit, the author of the whole of sanctification. Calvin takes the incorruptibility of the seed to be the answer to the hardest case, David's, who for a time laboured under such a stupor that not a spark of grace appeared: the seed may be stifled, but a live coal was hid under the ashes, and though Satan labours to root out whatever is of God in the elect, a hidden root remains. He also turns the clause against the Sorbonists, who allow that the will cannot desire what is right unassisted but imagine a motion of the Spirit leaving us free choice, and so draw merits out of our willing obedience; against them he holds that the Spirit's power is so effectual that it necessarily retains us in obedience, and continues to the last, so that inflexible perseverance is added to newness of life.

Clarke rejects the habitual reading as bringing the privileges of the heavenly birth very low indeed, and tells the story of the physiognomist who examined Socrates and pronounced him the most gluttonous and brutal old man he had met — and, when the pupils turned on him, was defended by Socrates: the principles of his science may be correct, for such I was, but I have conquered it by my philosophy. Will Christian divines, Clarke asks, allow the grace of Christ a sway not so extensive as the philosophy of a heathen who never heard of the true God? Wesley makes the new birth a living faith by which God continually breathes spiritual life into the soul, and the soul breathes out love and prayer.

Barnes gives both readings of the seed's owner — that his may refer to the man, the principle being now properly his own, or to God, who implanted a germ of divine origin — and reports that Robinson, Macknight and Lucke take the second, which he thinks true; as to what the seed is, Augustine, Clemens and Grotius take it for the word of God, but Barnes will not, since what abides in a Christian's heart is not the naked word but that word made vital by the Spirit. He takes cannot to mean a certainty as absolute as physical impossibility that the renewed will not be characteristically sinners. Robertson agrees the seed is God's, quoting Vincent's phrase for it, the divine principle of life, and says the English is a mistranslation: the present infinitive can only mean he cannot go on sinning, not that he cannot commit a sin, for which the aorist would have been used — and a great deal of false theology has grown out of a misunderstanding of the tense.

debates.question: In what sense can one born of God not sin?

positions.position: the tense decides it — the present infinitive means he cannot go on sinning, and much false theology has come of missing this
a certainty as absolute as physical impossibility that the renewed will not be characteristically sinners
not habitually only — that reading brings the heavenly birth very low, lower than a heathen philosopher's mastery of his vices
because the Spirit's power is so effectual that it necessarily retains the elect in obedience, against the Sorbonist notion of a motion that leaves free choice

outliers.note: refuses to resolve the tension by choosing a side, treating the man caught between the two sayings as the real subject of the passage and closing off only the claim to sinlessness

themes: the contradiction between this verse and the confession of sin
whose seed remains, and what it is

10.pericope_label: In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil

schools.summary: Cyril reads the verse as a warning against a doctrine rather than a life. He will not tolerate those who give a wrong meaning to the saying about the children of God and of the devil, as if there were by nature some men to be saved and some to be lost; we come into that sonship not of necessity but by choice. Judas was not by nature a son of perdition, for he would never otherwise have cast out devils in Christ's name, since Satan does not cast out Satan; nor would Paul have turned from persecuting to preaching. The adoption is in our own power, he says, quoting the word that to as many as received him he gave power to become children of God — not before their believing but from it were they counted worthy to become such by their own choice.

Gill uses the verse to separate two things often run together: adoption is an act of God's sovereign will, secret in his own heart and antecedent to regeneration, so that regeneration and faith do not make men the children of God but manifest them to be so — adoption entitles them to the inheritance, regeneration gives them the nature of children, and that not to the world but to themselves and other saints. Calvin reads the manifestation in the other direction: those claim a place among the children of God in vain who do not prove themselves such by a holy life, though he does not mean they are so manifested as to be recognised by the whole world, only that the fruit of adoption always appears in the life; since all whom God calls he regenerates by his Spirit, newness of life is a perpetual evidence of adoption. He also explains why the whole of righteousness can be summed up in a single duty, since the love of God holds the first place but love toward men depends on it, so the two are often put one for the other, a part for the whole.

Henry commends the injunction from its antiquity, since it came among the principal parts of practical Christianity: we should love the Lord Jesus and value his love, and consequently love all the objects of it.

Clarke calls it a fearful text and says we shall stand or fall by it whatever our creed may say; on the second half he allows no narrow construction, since God made of one blood all the nations of men, so that all are of one family and consequently brethren. Wesley marks the turn, that here the writer passes from the general proposition to one particular.

Barnes takes the sentence as a test of character with two parts, doing righteousness and loving the brethren, and suspects the singular pronoun intimates that an important part of righteousness consists in brotherly love; he reports the variant between message and commandment in the next verse and thinks it not material which is followed. Robertson calls this the line of cleavage obvious to all, comparing the Pharisees who claimed Abraham while their conduct showed them children of the devil, and remarks that it is not a popular note with an age that wishes to remove all distinction between Christians and the world; he notes that the word for message occurs in the New Testament only here and at the opening of the letter, and that the charge goes back to Cain and Abel.

debates.question: Are the children of God and of the devil such by nature?

positions.position: no — the adoption is in our own power, as Judas casting out devils and Paul turning from persecution both show
the manifestation is by fruit, not by nature: all whom God calls he regenerates, so newness of life is the perpetual evidence of adoption
adoption is an act of sovereign will, secret and antecedent to regeneration, which only manifests what adoption has already made

outliers.note: notes that the sharpness of the division is unfashionable, calling it not a popular note with an age that wishes to remove all distinction between Christians and the world

themes: whether the two families are so by nature
the message heard from the beginning

12.pericope_label: Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one; marvel not if the world hate you

schools.summary: Gill explains why the example comes in here: brotherly love is illustrated by its contrary, and Cain was the first instance both of hating a brother and of fratricide, a very detestable one, by which the writer would dissuade men from so abominable a practice. He also gives the history of the world's hatred — the enmity began upon the fall, between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent, showed itself in Cain, appeared when Ishmael persecuted Isaac, and continued when the Jews persecuted the prophets and hated Christ, so that this is the common lot of all who will live godly. Calvin uses the example to correct a mistaken account of holiness: men ever blunder as to the way of living because they make holiness consist of fictitious works, and while they torment themselves with trifles they think themselves doubly acceptable to God, as the monks who proudly call their mode of living a state of perfection. What the apostle testifies is that this righteousness alone is approved by God, that we love one another, and that the devil reigns where hatred, envy and enmity prevail.

Clarke turns the principle on a larger crime, asking who they are who through pride, lust of power and gain murder each other in wars and political contentions — they too are of the wicked one, and to justify the principle or excuse the abettors of such wars is as vain as it is wicked, since the message sent to man from the beginning was love one another and love your enemies, which surely does not mean blow out their brains. On the world's hatred he reads the verse as a lesson to the church preparatory to martyrdom, since neither justice nor mercy is to be expected from enemies of God, who are either full of malice and envy or else specious and hollow; he closes with a line of verse, that a foe to God was ne'er true friend to man. Wesley asks whether the brother was killed for any fault, and answers that it was just the reverse — he was killed for his goodness.

Robertson makes the verb harsher than our version does — an old word for slaughtering, to cut the throat like an ox in the shambles, occurring elsewhere in the New Testament only in the Revelation — and notes that the interrogative is an unusual construction meaning for the sake of what; he observes that the motive assigned is not in the narrative itself but an addition to it, though one that accords with what the letter to the Hebrews says of Abel's offering. On the following verse he notes that the imperative is present and negative, so the sense is not do not begin to wonder but cease wondering. Barnes reaches the same conclusion about the murder more quietly, that a large part of the crimes of the earth have been caused by want of brotherly love, and nothing but love would be needed to end them; and he puts the emphasis on the pronoun in the next verse, since as Cain hated his brother without cause, so they were not to think it strange that the world hated them likewise — the Saviour having introduced both subjects in the same connexion, and told the disciples that the world hated him before it hated them.

debates.question: Where does the account of Cain's motive come from?

positions.position: it is an addition to the narrative of Genesis, though one in accord with what Hebrews says of Abel's offering
it is the ordinary working of envy, and a specimen of the want of love that has caused a large part of the crimes of the earth

outliers.note: extends the verse from private hatred to organised war, holding that those who make and excuse wars of ambition are of the wicked one on the same principle as Cain

themes: the motive assigned for the murder
why the world’s hatred is unsurprising

14.pericope_label: We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren

schools.summary: Cyril quotes the phrase for its speed: the righteous were many years in pleasing God, but what they gained by long well-pleasing Christ bestows in a single hour, and he who saved the robber on Golgotha after one hour of belief will save any believer.

Gill sets out the death left behind. There is a moral death, lying in separation from God, in loss of the image of righteousness in which man was created, and in a servitude to sin which is itself death; and a legal death, the sentence under which all stand as considered in Adam. Regeneration is a resurrection, by which they pass to a life of sanctification, of justification, and of communion with Christ. Calvin says the argument is drawn from the sign and not the cause, since no one sincerely loves the brethren except he is regenerated by the Spirit, so love is a sure symbol of regeneration; but it would be preposterous to infer that life is obtained by love, which is in order of time posterior to it. He allows the milder claim, that love makes us more certain of life, and answers it too: though faith is confirmed by all the graces of God as aids, its foundation is his mercy only — as when we enjoy the light we are certain the sun shines, and see it more clearly when its rays fall where we stand, yet even when no ray reaches us we are satisfied that it shines for our benefit.

Henry is chiefly concerned to say what this love is not. It is not a zeal for a party, nor an affection for — still less an affectation of — those who share our denomination. It supposes a general love to mankind, the law of Christian love being founded on the catholic law of loving one's neighbour as oneself; and mankind is to be loved on two accounts, as the excellent work of God made in resemblance of him, which is the reason assigned for punishing a murderer, and as beloved in some measure in Christ, the whole race having a Redeemer designed for it. Only then does it include a peculiar love to the Christian society, and that for her head's sake, believers being loved not so much for themselves as for the sake of God and Christ, who have loved them.

Clarke reads the verb as a change of residence, death and life being two kingdoms whose inhabitants may be removed from one to the other, and compares Paul's word about translation into the kingdom of the Son of his love; those addressed had once lived in the region and shadow of death and had crossed into a kingdom where life and love prevail. Wesley states it the other way: we could not love our brethren unless we were passed from death to life.

Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun, the Christian consciousness set against the unregenerate world, and the perfect tense — the passage has already been made, here on earth; he makes the distinction grammatically, that the conjunction gives the proof of the transition and not its ground. Barnes calls the test infallible and wonders it is not more used, since a man can judge whether he loves a Christian because he bears the image of the Saviour, and whether he can look beyond the bounds of his own sect and be pleased with the Christian character wherever it is found; on the other side he agrees with Clarke that the man who does not love remains dead in sins.

debates.question: Does love to the brethren establish our standing or only evidence it?

positions.position: only evidence it — the argument is from the sign, not the cause, and love is posterior in time to the life it proves
it is an infallible evidence, and one a man can apply to himself if he will look beyond the bounds of his own sect

outliers.note: grounds the particular love of Christians on a prior general love to all mankind, so that the catholic law of loving one's neighbour is the foundation of the narrower duty rather than its rival

themes: love as sign rather than cause

15.pericope_label: Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer; he laid down his life for us

schools.summary: Gill calls the hater a soul murderer, and locates the crime where the Sermon on the Mount locates adultery — he murders his brother in his heart, since not only taking life but causeless anger and malice breaks the sixth commandment; he also reports the versions that carry the words of God in the next verse and those reading simply his love to us. Calvin insists the charge is not hyperbolical, since we wish him to perish whom we hate: it does not matter that a man keeps his hands from mischief, for even wishing evil to befall a brother from someone else makes us murderers. On the example of Christ he is careful how far the comparison runs — our love is approved when we transfer the love of ourselves to our brethren, so that every one in a manner forgetting himself seeks the good of others, but we are far from equal to Christ and to require it would drive us to despair, so what is asked is that we follow his steps at a distance; nor is the benefit of our death the same, for God's wrath is not pacified by our blood.
Henry names the thing plainly as the condescension, the miracle and the mystery of divine love, that God would redeem the church with his own blood.

Clarke enters a caution against a use made of the clause about eternal life: it has been quoted to prove that no murderer can be saved, which the text does not say, and there have been many instances of men guilty of murder who found genuine repentance and mercy from him who prayed Father, forgive them. It is nevertheless an awful text, he says, for those who shed blood on frivolous pretences, or in wars which have their origin in the worst passions of the human heart. Wesley allows no middle ground — there is no medium between loving and hating a brother, and every degree of hatred is a degree of the same temper that moved Cain; and he makes the omission of the divine name in the next verse eloquent, comparing Mary at the tomb saying to the gardener, Sir, if thou hast borne him hence, since there is an emphatical language even in silence.

Barnes reads the charge as a statement about tendency rather than equivalence: the writer does not say a man who hates without killing is guilty to the same degree, but that the spirit which would lead to murder is present, and nothing is wanting but the removal of outward restraint — a fearful declaration, since there are then many real murderers on earth besides those detected. On the next verse he thinks the added words of God should never have entered the translation, since they would convey the idea that the divine nature suffered, and the original is more expressive without them; and he gives a principle for when the duty of dying for others applies, that we should do it where a greater good results from the sacrifice than from guarding our own lives, as a physician stays with a pestilence. Robertson notes that the compound noun for murderer goes back to Euripides and occurs in the New Testament only here and of Satan, and agrees that our laying down our lives has no atoning value as Christ's had but is a supreme proof of love.

debates.question: Does the clause mean that no murderer can ever be saved?

positions.position: no — the text does not say it, and there have been many instances of murderers who found genuine repentance and mercy
the statement is about present tendency rather than final destiny: the spirit of a murderer is there, and God judges men as he sees them in their hearts

outliers.note: reads the missing divine name as itself expressive, comparing Mary's unnamed him at the tomb — an emphatical language in silence, showing how wholly the thoughts were possessed by the subject

themes: hatred as murder in the heart
whether a murderer may be saved
the divine name absent from the text

17.pericope_label: Whoso hath this world's good and shutteth up his bowels of compassion

schools.summary: Gill takes the world's good to mean any share of the outward enjoyments of life, noting that one version renders the phrase as though it pointed at a man in high office who is both great and rich, though the words are not to be restricted so; of a man who has nothing to spare it is not required. On the second verse he says it is lawful and right to express love in words, especially to persons in distress, but that this must not be all, since it is of no avail to tell such a man to be warmed and filled while giving him nothing to warm and fill him with. Calvin draws four propositions out of the first verse: no one truly loves his brethren except he shows it whenever occasion occurs; every man is bound to assist so far as he has means; the necessity of each is to be seen to, since a man requires our aid precisely as he needs the food of which we have abundance; and no act of kindness is pleasing to God unless accompanied with sympathy. He presses the last, since many apparently liberal men do not feel for the miseries of their brethren; and on the second verse he notes that the word only is understood in the first clause, that word answers to truth and tongue to work, and that the apostle cannot be supposed to forbid affectionate speeches to brethren in distress but forbids us to content ourselves with them.

Clarke puts the first verse as a test: if we do not divide our bread with the hungry we would certainly not lay down our life for him, and hardheartedness and the love of God never meet. On the second he quotes a rabbinical saying to the same effect — if love consisted in word only, then love would cease as soon as the word was pronounced, and such was the love between Balak and Balaam, but if love consists not in word it cannot be dissolved, and such was the love of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and the patriarchs before them. Wesley adds two strokes of his own, that the very sight of want knocks at the door of the spectator's heart, and that the man here described shuts it up whether he is asked or not.

Robertson confirms the sense of the noun, which means livelihood rather than the principle of life, and finds the picture sharpened by the tense — an aorist replacing the present, the graphic slamming of the door of his compassion; the word rendered bowels means the nobler viscera, and the closing question is rhetorical, since it is the practical, not the speculative, that counts in the hour of need. On the second verse he makes the same qualification as Calvin, that kind words which comfort and cheer are not condemned, but warm words should be accompanied by warm deeds — a case where actions speak louder than words. Barnes explains why the seat of mercy is named, since that part is affected when the mind feels compassion, and states the argument plainly: if we ought to be willing to lay down our lives, we ought to make the far smaller sacrifices that relieve distress.

debates.question: Does the command against loving in word condemn kind words?

positions.position: no — the word only is understood, and the apostle cannot be supposed to forbid affectionate speeches to brethren in distress, but forbids contenting ourselves with them
no — comforting and cheering words are not condemned, but they must be accompanied by warm deeds

outliers.note: adds sympathy as a fourth requirement beyond the giving itself, holding that the liberal man who does not feel the misery he relieves has not satisfied the command

themes: words not forbidden but not sufficient

19.pericope_label: Hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him

schools.summary: Augustine takes up the question the previous verse leaves open: in what work, or in what truth, is the man known who loves God or his brother? He has already said where charity is perfected, in the laying down of a life for friends, and grants that nothing greater can be found. But since it is not perfect in all, he will not let a man despair in whom it is imperfect, provided that be already born which may be perfected — for once born it must be nourished, and by feeding of its own kind brought to maturity. So he asks instead where charity begins, and answers from the verse about the man who has this world's goods and closes his heart.

Gill reads the evidence as a cause known by its effect: loving one another in deed, the saints learn that they belong to God, who is truth itself, to Christ who is the truth, and to the gospel, which is the word of truth. Calvin accepts none of that as a foundation, though he welcomes it as a support. Charity does not yield the knowledge the apostle speaks of, as though from it we might extract the certainty of salvation; we learn our sonship no otherwise than as God seals his free adoption on the heart by his own Spirit, and as faith receives the sure pledge offered in Christ, so that charity is accessory, an inferior aid, a prop and not a foundation. He allows the appeal only because faith cannot exist without a clear conscience — not that certainty springs from one, but that union with God is really and not falsely felt where the Spirit manifests himself in our charity; and nobody should conclude that we must look to works in order to be sure.

Clarke makes the test turn on what a man can and cannot fake. Nobody can impose upon himself by imagining an affection he lacks; he may make empty professions to others, but whoever loves God or man knows it because he feels it, and an unfelt affection is mere word or tongue. This, he says, is the strongest and most infallible test of a man's Christianity. Wesley calls it a further proof by real, operative kindness, and adds a lexical observation worth keeping — that heart in this writer's vocabulary means conscience, a term never appearing in his writings.

Barnes explains the verb rendered assure, which properly means persuade, and is used of bringing over one who has unkind or prejudiced feelings, and so of conciliating and quieting; the sense is that by furnishing evidence of genuine piety we allay the agitations of the mind and soothe an accusing conscience. He does not pretend the accusation is baseless: a true believer never denies that much in his past might justly indict him, yet finds despite it that he is God's child, and rests satisfied that all will end well. Robertson notes that the verb for knowing is future — at any future emergency we shall come to know by this — and that the assurance is had in the very presence of God, because God understands us.

debates.question: Can love to the brethren give certainty of salvation?

positions.position: no — charity is accessory, a prop to faith and not a foundation; certainty comes from the Spirit sealing adoption on the heart
it is the strongest and most infallible test that can be given, since a man cannot deceive himself about what he feels
it quiets the accusation rather than answering it, allaying the agitations of a mind that has much to accuse it

outliers.note: shifts the question from where charity is perfected to where it begins, so that an imperfect love is treated as a thing born and needing nourishment rather than as no love at all

themes: in what work love is known
assurance as persuasion of the heart
whether the evidence is a foundation

20.pericope_label: If our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart

schools.summary: Gill puts the threefold office briefly: the inward witness accuses of the evil of sin, is as good as a thousand witnesses, and on its own testimony pronounces guilty. Calvin takes the comparison to be one of judgment specifically, God searching more minutely, and cites Paul's word that though he knew nothing against himself he was not thereby justified — for however attentive to his office he erred in many things and was through inadvertence ignorant of faults God perceived; the meaning is that since divine knowledge penetrates deeper than our own perception, no man can stand before him unless the integrity of his heart sustains him. He also answers the presumptuous, observing that the reprobate are sometimes sunk by Satan into such stupor that they no longer perceive their own evils, and that hypocrites, inebriated by a false conceit of their righteousness, feel no convictions at all — the answer being that hypocrites are deceived because they shun the light, the reprobate feel nothing because they have departed from God, and there is no security for a bad conscience except in hiding-places, whereas the apostle speaks of men whom God draws forth to the light.

Henry reads the verse as establishing a court and asserting its authority. The heart here is our self-reflecting judicial power, by which we take cognizance of our own dispositions and actions and pass sentence on our state toward God; it acts as witness, judge and executioner, and holds that office by divine appointment, the spirit of man being the candle of the Lord which searches the inward parts — conscience is God's vicegerent, calling the court in his name, and God is chief Judge in it. To the trembling soul he replies that the errors of the witness are not reckoned as acts of the court: ignorance, prejudice and presumption are faults of the officers or of a jury returning a false verdict, not of the judge. What is bound in a rightly constituted court is bound in heaven, so let the inward witness be well informed, be heard, and be diligently attended to.

Clarke says God knows every hypocritical winding and turning of the soul, tries the reins, and sees the deceitfulness we cannot see and could not comprehend if we could; being the just Judge he will condemn us more strictly than we can condemn ourselves. Wesley calls him an infinitely holier and more impartial Judge, so that there is no hope of hiding anything.

Robertson observes that the verb for condemning occurs only three times in the New Testament, and that the omniscience appealed to here is linked with divine love and sympathy rather than set against it; he quotes Brooke's remark that this difficult passage strikes the very centre of Christian truth. Barnes presses the corollary: we cannot purchase quiet by supposing God fails to see what troubles us, since he knows the sins we have forgotten and those we persuade ourselves are not sinful, and looks on all with less allowance than we do. He adds the distinction that keeps the verse usable, that the reference is less to our past lives than to our present deportment — in view of past guilt peace may be found by evidences of piety, but no external act will soothe a heart that condemns us for secret sin indulged now.

debates.question: Does a self-accusing heart prove that God condemns us?

positions.position: not necessarily — the errors of the witness are not acts of the court; ignorance and prejudice belong to the officers or the jury, not the judge
the reference is to present sin rather than past guilt: evidences of piety can quiet the past, but nothing quiets a heart condemning present indulgence
the verse speaks only of consciences God draws to the light — stupefied and self-flattering men feel nothing, and that silence proves nothing

outliers.note: reads the divine omniscience here as consoling rather than threatening, linking it with God's love and sympathy: God knows every secret in our hearts and understands us

themes: God as the greater witness and judge

21.pericope_label: If our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God

schools.summary: Gill is careful to say what an unaccusing heart is not: not the stupidity of mind found in men who have no sense of sin, nor the state of those past feeling whose consciences are seared, nor such purity of life that a believer's heart never reproaches him, since that perfection is not attainable here — what is meant is a conscience purged by the blood of Christ, which speaks peace and pardon. Calvin raises the objection this invites, who can be found whose heart reproves him in nothing, and answers that the godly are reproved in such a way that they may at the same time be absolved: they must be seriously troubled inwardly for their sins, so that terror may lead them to humility and self-hatred, but they presently flee to the sacrifice of Christ, where they have sure peace. He also shuts the door against hypocrites, repeating his guard against reading the condition as a ground — woe to us if we look on works, which have nothing in them but cause for fear — and explains the causal particle as marking an inseparable companion rather than a cause, as when one says that because the sun shines at midday there is more heat, though heat comes not from light.
Henry adds that such men come as children to a reconciled Father and may ask what they will.

Clarke sums it up: if we are conscious of our own sincerity, practising no deceit and using no mask, we can appeal to God and come boldly to the throne of grace. He identifies the commandments meant as loving God and loving our neighbour, the great commandments of both covenants, since whoever is filled with that love will do what pleases God — love being the very soul of obedience; and he notes that heart in these verses stands for conscience, as the Greek fathers interpret it, Origen and Oecumenius among them. Wesley describes the same faculty as duly enlightened by the word and Spirit of God, comparing our thoughts and words and works with that word and pronouncing that they agree.

Robertson agrees the clause is the converse of the one before it but no claim to sinlessness — it describes the consciousness of fellowship in God's presence, and the boldness it yields extends even to prayer; he finds no limitation in the form of the promise save complete fellowship with God, which means complete surrender of our will to his, and remarks that the answer may not come in the shape we expect but will be better. Barnes explains the noun as properly openness in speaking one's sentiments, and enters the same guard: the writer does not mean we have confidence toward God on the ground of what we do, as if it constituted a claim on his favour. On the promise he states two limits, that we ask in a proper manner and that the thing asked be such as God sees consistent to give, and adds that obedience is not the ground of being heard but the evidence that we are his children — a parent being disposed to favour dutiful children.

debates.question: Whose heart can be said not to condemn him?

positions.position: not the seared or the stupefied, and not the sinlessly perfect, but a conscience purged by the blood of Christ
the godly, who are reproved precisely so that they may be absolved, and who flee from that terror to the sacrifice of Christ

outliers.note: explains the causal particle as naming an inseparable companion rather than a cause — as heat accompanies the midday sun without coming from its light

themes: what an unaccusing heart is not
the limits of the promise in prayer

23.pericope_label: This is his commandment, that we believe and love; and he that keepeth his commandments dwelleth in him

schools.summary: Cyril dwells on the dignity of the title conferred: since God himself is called Faithful, as he is called Good and Almighty, a man receiving that name becomes partaker of a title of God.

Gill says the two are reduced to one because inseparable — where one is, the other is, since faith works by love. Calvin notes the singular for the same reason, that the writer does not separate faith from love but requires both, and calls the verse remarkable for defining briefly wherein the whole perfection of a holy life consists: God does not lead us through labyrinths but sets before us shortly what he approves, and in that brevity there is no obscurity. He fastens on the word name, which he takes of preaching, since few understand what it is to believe on Christ, but the only right faith embraces him as he is set forth in the gospel, so there is no faith without teaching. On the indwelling he sets the verse beside Paul's: Paul speaks of the certainty of gratuitous adoption sealed on our hearts, while this writer regards the effects the Spirit produces while dwelling in us — and whatever good works we do proceed from his grace, the Spirit being not obtained by our righteousness but freely given.

Henry breaks the believing into four acts: to discern what Christ is according to his name; to approve him in judgment as one wonderfully adapted to the whole work of salvation; to consent to him and acquiesce in him as our recoverer unto God; and to rely on him for the full discharge of that saving office. He explains why this is required of one who would prevail in prayer, since it is by the Son that we come to the Father — through his purchase our blessings come, through his intercession our prayers are heard.

Clarke states the content of the believing, that for the sake of his death we are justified from all things from which the law could not justify us, and adds that without a renewal of the heart love to God and man is impossible, and that renewal comes by Christ. On the indwelling he will not stop at inference: it was not by conjecture that Christians of old knew they stood in God's favour but by the testimony of his own Spirit, which is not only manifest by its effects but bears its own witness to its own indwelling, so a man knows he has it by direct witness as well as by fruits; how that testimony is given is inexplicable, as the wind blows where it lists, but every good man feels it. Wesley calls the double command all the commandments in one word, the greatest that ever issued from the throne of glory — if neglected no other can be kept, if observed all others are easy.

Barnes calls it his commandment by way of eminence, the injunction lying at the foundation of all obedience; on the indwelling he takes it to be known only by effects, since the Spirit enlightens the mind, elevates the affections, sustains in trial and quickens in duty, and none can determine that he dwells in them except by what is produced in the life. Robertson notes that the manuscripts divide between aorist and present for the verb of believing, a crisis or the continuous tenor of a life, and that the name stands for all that Christ is, what Westcott called a compressed creed; on the last verse he quotes Bede — let God be a home to thee, and be thou the home of God — and observes that this is the first mention of the Spirit in the letter, regretting that our English keeps the grammatical gender, reading which for whom.

debates.question: How does a man know the Spirit dwells in him?

positions.position: only by the effects — none can determine it except by what is produced in the heart and life
by direct witness as well as by fruits: the Spirit bears its own witness to its own indwelling, inexplicably but certainly
by the effects, as distinct from Paul's sealing of adoption — and those effects are themselves the Spirit's free gift, not our righteousness

outliers.note: reads the command to believe as the conferring of a title, since Faithful is one of God's own names and the believer becomes partaker of it

themes: what believing on the name is
